speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO SALT FISH MARKETS AND PRICES SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement on salt fish markets and prices support. At this time last year there was, particularly in Newfoundland, much doubt about salt fish market prospects for the 1950 catch. Today prospects and outlook for 1951 are, however, more optimistic.
Last year there was a substantial carryover of salted fish from 1949 still in merchants' hands. The government took action to help dispose of this fish and thereby to relieve the whole Canadian salted fish trade from the pressure of over-supply. We bought substantial quantities for distribution through relief agencies. The fisheries prices support board provided guaranteed prices to fishermen for the Labrador cure. The government undertook to review the results of the 1950 marketing season on shore fish as well, and the study covering returns received by the shore fishermen in Newfoundland is now under way.
At present, prospects for the 1951 season are encouraging. In the past year in Newfoundland all the 1949 carry-over and the 1950 catch have been sold. At present forward sales are being made for fish still in the sea-a marked contrast to the situation at this time last year. There is practically no carry-over of old fish. The world supply of salted fish is likely to be slightly under last year's production. Markets are more buoyant. I was able to announce only a few days ago the sterling convertibility arrangement for Newfoundland, so that the way has been cleared for sales to Europe. Arrangements have been made to permit full sales of Gaspe cured salted fish to Italy for dollars.
We understand that the Newfoundland salt codfish association will meet this month with the Newfoundland fishermen to set minimum prices, with an undertaking to meet 80709-198
together later in the year with the fishermen's groups to work out final payments. This brighter outlook for Newfoundland sales should strengthen the export position of the maritime and Quebec salt fish trades.
As to the 1951 season, therefore, with market prospects good, the prices support board could see no justification for general prices support action in salted fish. During the year there may be some localities where, because of poor fishing, or poor quality fish, returns may not prove adequate to the fishermen. That, however, is more a question of local relief than of national prices support action.
We, along with the departments of finance and trade and commerce, will continue to be ready to help overcome marketing difficulties abroad, should these arise, and to encourage the expansion of the domestic market. Keeping in touch with the market, however, should not put us in the fish business. The responsibility for production and marketing in the Labrador cure, as well as in others, rests with the industry itself, with both fishermen and merchants. It is only under special conditions that government action under the support act should be contemplated. There is, in our opinion, no need for such special action at this time.
I have on several occasions discussed in this house the alternatives to prices support -the constructive plans for future development of our fisheries, particularly on the Atlantic coast. I am greatly encouraged by the fact that joint federal-provincial fisheries development committees have been established in Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island. These committees are seriously studying the problems of these provinces, and I believe they will give us sound and practical advice towards securing a better-balanced fishing industry. This better balance is already being achieved by the fishing industry in the eastern provinces. In Newfoundland, while cod provides the basic income, fishermen's earnings from flatfish, salmon, lobsters, capelin, and herring are continuously growing. Improved fishing techniques are providing more such varieties and also better sizes for marketing. New mechanical driers are producing better standards of quality in salted fish. The industry has built, and is adding this year, several

Fisheries
new freezing plants for fillets. It has added oil and meal plants. It is such development we want to encourage.
In the meantime, and while the development committees prepare their recommendations, we are aiding by research and application the modernization of both the salted and the fresh and frozen fish trades in eastern Canada. For example, in Newfoundland this summer we shall have nine research board engineers-some engineering new fish plants, others checking present installations in freezing plants, in smokers, and in cod liver oil plants. We are installing a new experimental drier for light salted fish at Bay Bulls. We have arranged for two Nova Scotia long-liners to fish with their special techniques in Bonavista, both as an experiment and as a demonstration of techniques.
For the shore fishermen throughout eastern Canada we are expanding our assistance to help them modernize their vessels. The federal government assistance to the construction of draggers and long-liners is now applicable to Quebec and the Magdalens, as well as to the maritimes, and it can be made available to Newfoundland on agreement with the provincial government. The regulations have been changed to increase the assistance. Whereas the payments were formerly made ;o draggers or long-liners fifty-five feet and jp they are now available to vessels forty-five feet and up. This should greatly extend the scope of the grant, which is $165 per gross ton; and it is available to single fishermen or to groups.
We believe that the progress of our Atlantic fishing industry is dependent greatly on the successful application of modern techniques, both in fishing and in processing, in doing old things in better ways, or in doing new things -new methods of fishing, processing, and distributing. Federal assistance in these directions, rather than prices support, will redound to the long-run benefit of the fishermen and their families as well as to all the coastal communities.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 79, respecting Indians.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the bill carries I should like to make a further attempt to have two changes made in this legislation. The first concerns section 4, subsection 2, and the second concerns the question of allowing any Indian or band of Indians to appeal to the courts against a ministerial decision. These subjects have both been debated fully and I therefore do not intend to go over the ground of the discussion and present in full the merits of the case in support of the amendment which I propose to move. I wish as briefly as possible simply to outline the effects of the amendment, and then leave it to the decision of the house whether or not the amendment should be supported.
In the Indians of Canada we have over 125,000 subjects of His Majesty. Their whole future life is to be governed under the Indian Act, and they differ from the rest of us in that way. This House of Commons must direct its mind to the question whether or not we are giving justice to these Indians, whether we are doing everything we can to place them on a basis of equality and in a position to protect their rights.
With respect to section 4, it is desired by those of us who support the amendment which I am about to move that the Indians should be given the right to have a say in decisions which are taken affecting their whole status. Section 4 gives the governor in council the power to issue proclamations which would exempt from the provisions of the bill, except sections 37 to 41, any Indian or group of Indians or Indian band. Such proclamations may be issued without prior consultation with the band. There is nothing at all in the statute which makes it essential that the Indians themselves should be consulted before these proclamations are issued.

Anything affecting the status of Indians, anything affecting the question whether or not Indians should be on the Indian list, anything affecting the right or disability of Indians to obtain liquor, anything at all except the very narrow category of subjects dealt with in sections 37 to 41 involving surrenders of land, can be changed simply by a proclamation of the governor in council.
I wish to emphasize that it is not argued that the process by which these changes are made should be altered. It is not argued that it should require a further bill or further legislation to make the changes which the minister now contemplates will be made by proclamation. We realize fully that in administering the act, day to day problems will arise. There are problems of details. There may be problems affecting only one Indian or a small number of Indians, and it would not be appropriate to insist that each of these changes must necessitate a bill and all the legislative process of passing an act of parliament. It is perfectly proper to leave those things to be done by proclamation, but it is contended that before such proclamations are issued the consent of the Indians or the band concerned should be obtained.
That seems to me a very simple proposition, and there should not be an attempt to sidetrack it by saying this would mean a process of legislation every time it was desired to take any administrative action under this act. That is not the suggestion at all, and if the amendment were adopted no such result would follow. It would mean that the Indians themselves, who are so vitally affected, would have the safeguard that before their rights could be abridged, before any change could be made in their status which might have very serious consequences for them, must be first consulted and their consent obtained. I do not believe this house would pass a bill giving any government or minister power to change the status of a white person or white community in this country by proclamation without the requirement of prior consultation and consent on the part of the person or community whose status might be changed; nor do I think we should do that in connection with the Indians.
I am not moving the amendment formally at the moment, but the motion will be simply that the bill be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that the committee have power to amend it by inserting in section 4(2) the words "with the consent of the Indians or band concerned." That is all it is. It does not say that it has to be by any other process, or that it cannot be by proclamation. It simply says that the consent of the Indians or band concerned must first be obtained.
Indian Act
The other part of the amendment I intend to move relates to the right of Indians to appeal to the courts. I am not going to attempt a legal argument in any detail, but I think it was agreed yesterday by the minister and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), who has been the prime proponent of this amendment, that many administrative decisions and orders are made by the minister from which there is no right of appeal. To that extent the Indians are entirely different from and in an inferior position to the white population. Surely, if we are going to make them equal at all, one of the first respects in which we should make them equal is by giving them equality under the law with white citizens, one of whose most valuable rights is the right to free recourse to the courts whenever they think themselves aggrieved.
Under the Indian Act there are a number of instances in which the Indian, whose future and fortune can be vitally affected by administrative decisions made by the minister or his officials, has no recourse to the courts and no one further to whom he can appeal for the redress of grievances. This not only places the Indian in a position of inferiority, which he is entitled to resent and which in many cases he does resent, thereby imposing another barrier in the way of this equality we wish to create, but it is nothing short of an injustice to place and keep the Indian in this inferior position in comparison with the white citizens of this country. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton):
That the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house with instructions that such committee have power to amend the same by inserting in clause 4 (2) thereof, after the word "may" at line 18, the following words: "with the consent of the Indians or band concerned."
And further that such committee have power to amend the said bill by inserting the following as section 123:
"Nothing in this act or elsewhere shall in any way be deemed to remove, abridge or otherwise restrict the rights of Indians to full access to the courts of the land, and every Indian and every band of Indians shall have the full right to appeal to the appropriate court of the province which would otherwise have jurisdiction, from any decision of the minister hereunder."
And by renumbering present sections 123 and 124 as 124 and 125.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask that the amendment be not adopted by this house but that the bill in its present form be permitted to go into effect. With respect to section 4 and the non-existent section the hon. member would propose to add, from my point of view, as representing a riding in which there is a large number of Indians at various

Indian Act
stages of development, at the moment I would prefer that the discretionary power to bring into effect the provisions of section 4 should remain with the governor in council, advised, as it doubtless will be, by the experienced men in the Indian affairs branch. I would point out, though I admit this is not a strong argument, that should the governor in council make a mistake in the application of this act, upon that mistake being brought to its attention the last line of this section also permits the revocation of any such proclamation by the governor in council.
As for the addition of a section such as was so well asked for recently, by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), which would state as a fact what the minister has told us is now the law, I think the reply by the minister to the hon. member for Lake Centre should satisfactorily dispose of that argument. However, the point I wish to make at the moment I think is of considerable importance when considering this bill as a whole. This bill is far from perfect, as I am sure the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) would be the first to admit. But as yet its imperfections are largely unknown. Until we have some experience with the new sections of the bill we cannot say definitely where it has fallen short or where it may have gone too far. I took it upon myself to ask the minister in the committee whether, if this bill went through, he would undertake within a period of approximately two to ,hree years to call together, not necessarily i committee of this house but a representative group of Indians from right across Canada, similar to that which was called together at the end of February last, with a view to going into the way this act has operated so that such corrections as might be found necessary could be made on the basis of experience and not conjecture. May I read into the record this part of the minister's reply:
Now, I did not go the step further, and tell the conference that they would be reassembled in two years' time, but I am prepared to give the committee the assurance, within the limits stated by Mr. Applewhaite, that it would be the intention of this government to invite representative Indians to another conference similar to that held in February last.
Under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I submit, and I think I have the interests of the Indians fully at heart, as I know the member for Kamloops has, that the best way in which we can show our desire to make improvements for the Indians of Canada is to pass this bill, which has been thoroughly investigated by a committee, and get it on the statute book.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to illustrate that the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has not been without some justification in making this motion, I should like to read into the record a press report which appeared not so long ago. As I recall it, it appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, and the heading is "Act threatens extinction of Indian people." There is a question mark following that title. The article reads:
A three-man delegation from the Six Nations Indian reservation near Brantford warned here yesterday that passage of the Indian Act in its present revised form would threaten the Indian people with extinction in two years' time.
They said if the act became law, the Indians across Canada would become "bitter enemies" of the present federal government.
The delegation centred its fire on the compulsory enfranchisement clause of the act.
Under this clause, a government appointed committee may enfranchise an Indian whether or not he has applied for such enfranchisement. Once he is given the vote, the Indian loses special reservation rights such as free schooling, free hospitalization and exemption from taxes.
The delegation objected to section 4 of the acr giving the minister (in this case, citizenship and immigration minister Walter Harris) unlimited powers with no recourse of appeal.
Criticism was also voiced of the provision under which an Indian who asks for the vote must sign a waiver eliminating his exemption from taxation.
Members of the delegations who saw Mr. Harris, were: E. P. Garlow, chief councillor of the Six Nations Indian council; A. C. Moses, council secretary, and James Powless, councillor.
Perhaps these men were extreme in their views, but I am concerned lest the opinion which is expressed by these men is the opinion held by altogether too many Indians across Canada. Consequently, I am not sure that the member for Kamloops has not done the country a service in bringing this matter to the attention of the house. I do not see why there should not be a provision giving the Indians, when threatened with the application of these clauses of the act, the right to defend their rights in court against the will of the department.
Notwithstanding what the minister has said, and notwithstanding what the past history has been, the Indians do not possess an effective right to appeal to the courts in respect of matters of this kind. One of the main reasons is that the average Indian on the average reserve in Canada is by no means a wealthy man. As a matter of fact I believe it could be safely said that the average Indian on our reservations is a very poor man. The average band on a reserve would have much difficulty in raising sufficient money to enable any Indian to defend successfully his rights in court. Since this condition obtains it must be obvious that whether or not an Indian has

the legal right, he has not the financial strength to enable him to defend successfully his case in any court.
I should feel much better about the whole situation if some commission or some body were set up which would take a part comparable with that which is taken for a veteran by the pensions advocate. The government would put at the disposal of the Indian, men who would be highly trained, and whose business it would be to defend the Indian. By appointing such a commission the government would acknowledge the disability under which the Indian now labours, through no fault of his own, and would express complete willingness that everything should be done to defend the position of the Indian. I think, Mr. Speaker, that anything less than that is not sufficient in our time, having in mind the condition which obtains throughout our Indian population at present. I would be prepared, therefore, to support the amendment moved by the member for Kamloops.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken I should like to say a few words more as regards this important measure.
We of this parliament are now taking a last look at Bill 79, an act respecting Indians. We have toiled long and earnestly. The task we have wrestled with has not been, and is not now, an easy one.
The problem connected with Canada's Indians, admittedly a highly complex one, complex if not baffling, is not a problem of this generation's making. We have inherited it; it has been left on our doorstep, so to speak. I urge upon all, both non-Indian and Indian, patiently to bear this important fact in mind.
There is too much of a tendency I fear on the part of a number of our Indians and non-Indians to feel unkindly toward each other. There is no justification whatsoever for any bitterness between the two groups of Canadians. We must simply recognize that we have a difficult problem to solve, and we must face this problem frankly and honestly, and without passion, and do the very best we can to solve it in the interests of all.
No blame can be attached to the men and women of our time for the mistakes that may or may not have been made in days now gone, or for the weaknesses that may have manifested themselves in the relations between the two groups. On the other hand no credit is due us for the noble achievements of our fathers, both Indian and nonIndian, whose efforts preceded ours-and there were noble achievements, on both sides.
In debates centring around the Indian Act much has been said which might seem to reflect upon the fathers of our nation, both Indian and non-Indian. In so far as any such impression as that might have been gained through anything I have said, I wish here to disavow any intention of reflecting in any way upon the men and women of earlier times in Canada. I believe that on the whole they did the best they could, and, as I have said noble achievements must be credited to them.
Understanding, forbearance, prudence and skill were manifested by Indian and nonIndian in those dangerous days, while we were learning to adjust ourselves to each other. And. there was confidence, hope and faith on both sides. Splendid efforts were made both by Indian and non-Indian, and those efforts in great measure were crowned with success-a success for which all of us have cause to be deeply grateful to our forebears.
To realize how much truth there is in what I have just said, all we need to do is
fMr. Speaker.]
to recall the difference which generally prevailed in the feelings between Indians and non-Indians in Canada, and the feelings which prevailed in relations between Indians and non-Indians in the United States. My father and mother came to Canada from the United States in 1892 and were well qualified to impress upon me how splendidly different was the situation in Canada from that in the United States. My father told me that while he was in Idaho, where he lived before he came to Alberta, he never went into the wilds without having a rifle and a six-shooter within reach. When they came to Canada they found there was no danger whatsoever. The mounted police seemed to have everything well in hand and the Indians seemed- to be happy that they had.
It rests upon our generation to do its full part in the light of the knowledge and facilities at our disposal. We have far greater knowledge and we have far more facilities and therefore we can give the Indians far better times in the days to come if we only realize how to use the resources which have been placed at our disposal by the Almighty.
I feel we in this parliament have done a workmanlike job. I want the Indians who may be reading this to know that that is how I feel.
Recently I read to the house an excerpt from an article entitled, "Who is an Indian?" which was reprinted from the Albertan of Calgary, Alberta, of April 25, 1951. This article is signed by John L. Laurie, secretary of the Indian Association of Alberta. I want to give Mr. Laurie all the credit which is his due. I know of no man who has more selflessly and indefatigably exerted himself in the interests of better times for the Indians than this same John L. Laurie. He is a schoolteacher by profession and has done his work for the Indians on the side. He risked his health and in fact has impaired his physical condition to a dangerous point. I believe the Indians of Canada could well afford to set up monuments to Mr. Laurie on every reservation from coast to coast. In the opening paragraph of this -statement, Mr. Laurie said:
The new Indian Act, in its present revised form, is an excellent piece of legislation. The government has met the most serious objections of the Indians themselves, and seems genuinely interested in giving these people a charter that will assure their steady progress and development.
I agree fully with every syllable of that statement. This does not mean that I believe the bill is all that could be desired, neither does it mean that I think the attitude of the minister, of the department or of the government is all that could be desired. I am not sure that the position of the Indians

is appreciated adequately even yet. I think the minister has done literally wonders in training and conditioning himself since he took office, and he is entitled to those words at least, if not to stronger words. But he will be the first to maintain that there might be room for improvement.
As an illustration of what I have just said about appreciation may I refer to the case of the Six Nations Indians who are very unhappy about the situation generally at the present time. May I read to the house a statement which was made on May 11, 1914, by the Hon. Frank Oliver, as reported on page 3537 of Hansard. The Hon. Frank Oliver was a prominent Liberal and one of the finest men ever produced by western Canada. His words are worthy of note by the minister and his department and by the people generally throughout Canada. He said:
But there are bands of the Six Nations Indians located on the Grand river in Ontario who, I maintain, are in a different legal position from any Indian bands who are native to the country. These Indian bands on the Grand river had their original home in the United States. At the close of the war of the revolution they emigrated to Canada and were given lands under a special treaty, not as subjects of Great Britain, but as allies of Great Britain, and I maintain that the holding of these Six Nations Indians on the Grand river is of such a kind that this parliament has no right to interfere with it. I admit that parliament has the power to interfere with the rights of Indians under treaty made with this government, but I say that this parliament has no right to interfere with a treaty made between the imperial government and the Six Nations Indians.
It is to be granted that this creates a difficult situation for the minister and the department, but difficult situations have been met in former times. After all, the men of our country who have got along with the Six Nations Indians since Canada became a nation have in the main shown pretty well the way in which we can get along with these great people without violating any of the things which they hold sacred.
There are other considerations which I have referred to and which I believe I should elaborate on to some extent before I resume my seat in what is perhaps the closing speech of this debate. I have referred to the fact that traditionally the Indians revere the memory of the great white god who visited America. In order to appreciate the Indians and in order to appreciate the position of the Six Nations Indians we have to bear that fact in mind. I wonder if Canadians generally appreciate the historical and religious background of the Six Nations Indians, and also the background of the other Indians in this country?
May I read from a document which was placed in my hands by the Six Nations 80709-199
Indian Act
Indians which rather emphasizes what I have just said. This document is entitled, "Traditional History of the Confederacy of the Six Nations" and was prepared by a committee of the chiefs and presented by Duncan C. Scott, F.R.S.C., and read on May 16, 1911.
I read from page two as follows:
There is no doubt in the mind of the writers of this preface that many - of the ancient traditions of the Six Nations have become much modified and some have been long relegated to oblivion owing to the fact that in the earlier history of these people there were for a long time no members of the band capable of rendering these traditions in writing and thus preserving them intact to their posterity.
It is, however, a noteworthy fact that the league of the Five Nations confederacy (now known as the Six Nations) as constituted centuries ago by De-ka-nah-wi-deh and his associates, has been maintained in accordance with the rules of the confederacy as laid down by the founder of the league; and that the installation of the lords or chiefs as rulers of the people, laid down in these unwritten rules hundreds of years ago, is still strictly observed and adhered to by the chiefs of the Six Nations and people.
If a person weighs those words carefully he will look upon the unrest which presently exists among the Six Nations Indians with a considerable amount of sympathy. Who might this De-ka-nah-wi-deh be? I am told that the meaning of the word is "miracle child" which immediately suggests our Saviour, the Lord. Was it Christ? It could have been. Christ could have come over to America after he was resurrected. As far as I can see, there is no sufficient reason why anyone should suppose he could not have done that or did not do so.
May I turn to the Bible for a minute or two in connection with this matter? I am going into some detail here because I do believe that there is danger of unhappy relations existing between the minister and the department and the Six Nations Indians, and that probably these fine people may not be properly understood. Consequently I am holding up the progress of affairs this afternoon so that this other aspect of the matter may be considered by the Canadian people. We find that in the book of John, chapter 10, verse 16, there appear the following words-and Christ is speaking:
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; andj there shall be one fold and one shepherd.
At no place in scripture is it indicated where Christ went to find these other sheep which were not of the fold in Palestine. Who is to say that the people of America were not these sheep, and that Christ did not come to these people? No one can definitely say that could not have been the case. May I now turn to Matthew, chapter 15,

Indian Act
verse 24, for a statement which also has some bearing on this matter. It is referring to Christ and reads:
But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
If it should be found that the Indians are descendants of a branch of the Israelites, then considerable meaning can be derived from those two passages of scripture.
Having said as much as this, I think I should give some evidence from the history of America, It will take me about five minutes to do so, and will be of value to those who may read these remarks and desire to check the validity of what I have been saying. There are about fifteen or twenty great writers who have given much attention to the aborigines of America seeking to find out what their beliefs were, and what their origin was. Among these are A. H. Verrill, Lord Kingsborough, H. H. Bancroft and the Marquis de Nadaillac. I should like to give brief quotations from the works of each of these men before I close. Let us begin with A. H. Verrill. He wrote a work entitled "Under Peruvian Skies", published in 1930. In his works we find these words:
Among the Mexicans, the Mayas and the preIncan and Incan people of Peru there was a persistent, universally believed tradition of a bearded white man who visited their lands, taught them their civilizations and religions and then mysteriously disappeared. The tradition tells of this bearded god having reached Mexico and Yucatan in a "magic ship," and the tradition of the first Inca- "Manko Kapak"-having appeared from lake Titicaca and having declared himself the "Son of the Sun."
Lord Kingsborough in his monumental work, "Antiquities of Mexico" in nine volumes, published from 1830 to 1848, has this important statement to make bearing on the subject I am discussing:
The Aztecs have a tradition of a god suffering and crucified named Quetzalcoatl, and of one preceding Him to prepare the way and call them to repentance. Tezcaltlipoca offered Him a cup, calling him "my Son," of his unwillingness to taste and weeping bitterly after having drunk its contents; forsaking temporal kingdoms for spiritual, being called away by the Father. At His departure there were four earthquakes. He promised to return again and redeem his people.
Anyone who cannot see quite clearly indications of the story of Christ there will probably be unfamiliar with the story of Christ as given in our bible. May I turn now to H. H. Bancroft in his rather remarkable work, "Native Races", in five volumes, published in 1883. I should like to refer to the following passage:
Although bearing various names and appearing in different countries, the American culture-heroes all present the same general characteristics. They are all described as white, bearded men, generally clad in long robes; appearing suddenly and mysteriously upon the scene of their labours, they at [Mr. Blackmore.l
once set about improving the people by instructing them in useful and ornamental arts, giving them laws, exhorting them to practice brotherly love and other Christian virtues, and introducing a milder and better form of religion: having accomplished their mission, they disappear as mysteriously and unexpectedly as they came; and finally, they are apotheosized and held in great reverence by a grateful posterity. In such guise or on such mission did Quetzalcoatl appear in Cholula, Votan in Chiapas, Wixepecocha in Oaxaca, Zamna, and Cukulcan with his nineteen disciples, in Yucatan, Gucumatz in Guatemala, Viracocha in Peru, Sume and Paye-Tome in Brazil, the mysterious apostle mentioned by Rosales in Chile and Bochica in Colombia.
There are some of the names by which this great white god is known in various parts of America. In every ease this great white god possesses the same characteristics. They are closely similar to those possessed by De-ka-nah-wi-deh, who is revered in the traditions of the Six Nations.
May I quote one more short passage on this matter, this time from de Nadaillac's work, "Prehistoric America", published in 1885. There will be those of course who will think that the Indians got these ideas about Christ from missionaries who came to this country. The following passage will disabuse the minds of such. It reads:
No dissemination of merely Christian ideas since the conquest is sufficient to account for these myths.
The Marquis de Nadaillac has given thorough study to this matter and supports his statement adequately. There is no need here to refer to the elaboration in which he indulges in his work. Those who are interested can get the work. Some of these books are in our parliamentary library, where those interested can study these matters themselves.
Having said thus much, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that we may come more and more to appreciate the Indians and sympathize with them, I will close by saying that our generation will do well to take up the Canadian Indians as a solemn obligation and a sacred responsibility.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we
were considering the customs tariff resolution the other evening the hon. member for Eglinton, the hon. member for Acadia, and perhaps some other members, asked that an opportunity should be provided to discuss the Torquay agreement. The hon. member for Greenwood asked me if any of the items in the customs tariff resolution were related in any way to the Torquay agreement, and I told him they were not. I promised at that time to take up with my colleagues the question as to whether it would not be desirable to afford an opportunity to consider the agreement. Hon. members will have seen on the order paper a motion in the name of the Prime Minister asking that the Torquay agreements and related matters be referred to the banking and commerce committee. If it meets with the convenience of the house, I would hope that we might be able to bring on that motion for consideration early next week at which time members who wish to discuss the question generally might do so. Then the motion could be passed and the agreement referred to the banking and commerce committee. There Mr. Hector McKinnon, who was the acting head of the delegation, would be available to hon. members for detailed discussion. But I repeat what I said to the hon. member for Green-' wood the other evening, that the particular items here are not in any way related to those agreements.

There are two matters I should like to place before the minister. The first has to do with this matter of including in item 409f sprinkler irrigation systems. We had some discussion about that type of equipment when this resolution was last up for consideration, and I find now that there was considerable discussion in the house at other sessions. For example, on November 10, 1949, at page 1630 of Hansard, we find a statement by the parliamentary assistant in reply to a question raised concerning sprinkler irrigation systems, in which he said:
I do not think that this matter comes under the Department of Finance, but I am quite sure that if this new equipment-
He was referring to sprinkler equipment, -which apparently is being used so successfully in western Canada, reaches any real volume of sales it will not be very long before the industrialists of eastern Canada will be using Canadian aluminum to satisfy the demand. That is perhaps the only argument we have for the retention of such an item.
There the parliamentary assistant was arguing that if Canadian manufacturers could 80709-199J
Customs Tariff
build up their resources so they could manufacture this equipment and sell it at reasonable prices, they were to be encouraged to do so. The following year this equipment was again discussed, and at page 2579 of Hansard for May 17, 1950, we find the parliamentary assistant saying:
The question was raised a year ago by the hon. member for Kamloops and, I think, the hon. member for Calgary East, with respect to the complete portable irrigation equipment. That situation has been adjusted; there is an ample supply available in Canada today. I am told, however, that there is a temporary shortage of sprinkler heads. This has been brought to the attention of the department and they are trying now to see that a satisfactory supply is made available; or if that cannot be done an adjustment in regard to the tariff will be carefully considered. There is no adjustment in this tariff.
There the parliamentary assistant was enunciating government policy as being the encouragement of the production of these systems in Canada, just as had been done the preceding ye.ar. As the minister knows, Canadian firms are now in a position to supply the need. Then the hon. member for Kamloops asked:
Then do I understand that if an adequate supply of sprinkler heads cannot be made available domestically the department will consider an adjustment in the tariff for future years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is one of the items for discussion at Torquay this summer.
There we find the Torquay negotiations coming into the picture. The other evening the minister explained that Canada had not been successful in getting any consideration from the Americans on this type of equipment in the negotiations at Torquay, and of course such equipment is not included in the agreement between the two countries. It does seem to me that in view of these facts, first that the producers of equipment have been led to believe that they should get themselves in a position to produce these sprinkler systems, and second that Canada did not get any concession in this connection from the Americans at Torquay, in all fairness these sprinkler irrigation systems should not have been included in the changes set out in item 409f, and I would hope the minister might see his way clear to withdraw that type of equipment from these changes.
The other matter about which I would like a statement is the proposed dumping duty on British cars. For some time these cars have been coming in without the imposition of a dumping duty, but some weeks ago a statement was made that the provision which relieved them of the danger of having a dumping duty levied was to be withdrawn at either the end of April or the end of May.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The end of May.

Customs Tariff

What is to be the policy? It does seem to me that the importation of these British cars has served a very useful purpose. I know many hundreds of them have been imported into Vancouver, where they have been sold at prices very much below the prices of cars made on this continent. This business has greatly helped the British, in that as a result they are in a much better position to purchase Canadian goods. I would doubt the wisdom of stopping that trade by means of a dumping duty. I would ask the minister to deal with these two questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has pointed out, the question of the sprinkler systems has been under consideration for two or three years. I understand they are a relatively new development. When, the matter was first raised in the house I think, they were very new as far as Canada is concerned, and I believe they are still quite new here. My information is that it is only recently that manufacturers here have commenced to manufacture this type of equipment. I had the officers of my department make a very careful investigation of the business, the sources of supply and that sort of thing. It was clearly demonstrated to my satisfaction that this equipment was used primarily in agriculture rather than for irrigating golf courses and things like that, and I therefore came to the conclusion that it came within the broad group which Mr. Ilsley announced in 1944 would be admitted to Canada free of duty.
Before we decided to take it off the list and admit it free we did ask our negotiators at Torquay to ascertain whether the Americans would be prepared to give anything in return for such a concession. We found they were not; and rather than allow an industry to be created in Canada behind a tariff wall which might be even more difficult to remove at a later date, we came to the conclusion that the tariff should be removed this year; and to that decision I think we would have to adhere. In the case of the one manufacturer in particular whom I saw personally, and with whom I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is acquainted, I am looking into the question of whether some relief can be afforded in connection with the parts which were imported prior to the introduction of the budget, but that is still under investigation.
As to the question of the dumping duty, I am very happy that my hon. friend has raised the question because I should like to make a fairly comprehensive statement as to the position of the dumping duty, more particularly as it relates to British motor cars. As the committee is probably aware,

the basic provision of Canada's anti-dumping legislation is section 6 (1) of the Customs Tariff, which reads as follows:
In the case of goods exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value or the value for duty of the goods as determined under the provisions of the Customs Act, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such goods, on their importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the goods for export and the said value for duty thereof; and such special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such goods although not otherwise dutiable.
As the committee again will probably recall, Canada's first anti-dumping legislation was introduced in 1904 by the government of the day headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Details of that legislation have been amended from time to time, but the present clause is substantially as it was established in 1904, and subsequently maintained by other low-tariff Liberal prime ministers. The antidumping legislation, as it will be appreciated, made it possible for tariff rates to be reduced greatly without leaving Canadian producers open to unfair competition from dumped goods. The committee will recall that as long as an article is imported into Canada at no less than the fair market value in the country of origin, the dumping duty does not apply.
The provision introduced in 1904 complemented Sir Wilfrid's policy of consistent tariff reduction, and indeed during the forty-five years since then the anti-dumping clause has formed an integral part of the traditional Liberal policy of having low tariffs, but at the same time not sacrificing Canadian industry and agriculture to unfair competition from abroad. As the committee is aware, automobiles enter Canada from the United Kingdom free of customs duties, as well as from other British preferential sources. I suggest it would be difficult to defend this exemption from the regular duty if dumping in Canada were to be permitted permanently.
Canada's anti-dumping duties have never affected the importation of British automobiles appreciably. They are not applicable unless dumping occurs, and normally British cars are not dumped in Canada. However, in 1948, home market values of British automobiles in terms of sterling were high in relation to the price of Canadian cars at the then exchange rate of $4.03 to the pound. Consequently British motor vehicle producers found it necessary to export at prices below the home market value if they were to expand their sales in Canada to the desired extent. Thus if Canada's anti-dumping legislation had

been kept in force and had been applied rigidly in 1948, it would have had an adverse effect on the sales of British cars in Canada. In view of this situation the Canadian government took action by order in council to suspend the application of section 6 of the customs tariff in respect of automobiles. This suspension also applied to some other kinds of goods where the circumstances were similar.
Under the circumstances that prevailed in 1948 and early 1949, there was a real need for this action. However, since the devaluation of sterling in September, 1949, there has been no need for British automobile manufacturers to dump their products in Canada. Most of them, virtually all of them, have not done so. Accordingly the reinstitution of the Canadian anti-dumping provisions under present circumstances will not affect the principal makes of British automobiles at all. My information is that there is only one or two of the more expensive cars which, at the present time, would be affected. I have no doubt that will be rapidly corrected. As I say, there may be one or possibly two British companies who may be affected to some extent, but they can quite easily conform to the provisions of the law.
When the anti-dumping duties were suspended in 1948 the suspension applied to imports from any country. The suspension could not be limited exclusively to British cars, because the general agreement on tariffs and trade forbids discrimination in matters of this sort. However, the need to make the suspension non-discriminatory did not occasion any difficulty until recently because imports of cars from the United States and certain other foreign countries were limited by quota under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act. As I have pointed out to this house on other occasions, that gives a most decided advantage to the British motorcar manufacturers.
Since the government suspended automobiles from the anti-dumping provisions in 1948, conditions have changed in two important respects. The import quota restrictions have been removed from cars from the United States, and sterling has been devalued by about thirty per cent. British cars can now be sold in Canada readily without resort to dumping. There is no longer any need to continue the suspension of dumping duties in order to help imports from Britain. Moreover, there is a danger that if these exemptions were continued indefinitely they might be abused by exporters in other countries.
The following considerations, Mr. Chairman, are I think relevant to the government's
Customs Tariff
decision to terminate the suspension of the anti-dumping provisions in respect of automobiles as of May 31 next.
First, after the devaluation of sterling in September, 1949, it was no longer necessary for British automobiles to be dumped in Canada. Second, imports of United States and other foreign cars are no longer subject to any quantitative restrictions. Accordingly, continuation of the suspension of anti-dumping duties might benefit foreign cars more than those from Britain. Third, if the suspension were continued indefinitely, Canadian automobile manufacturers would be convinced, and might be able to convince others, that they had a legitimate grievance because their competitors would be able, if they so desired, to dump in Canada at will. This would make it difficult to defend the continued free entry of British automobiles. Fourth, the action which the government took in 1948 to suspend the application of antidumping legislation to automobiles and certain other products was regarded from the start as a temporary measure rather than a permanent change in government policy respecting dumping. There was no intention of continuing this suspension any longer than required in order to deal with a particular condition that no longer exists.

Mr. Chairman, some months ago I had something to say about these dumping duties on cars, so I was interested in hearing the minister's remarks this afternoon. But I still cannot go along with him in his explanation of the reasons for reimposing these dumping duties. If British competition in the form of these small cars was hurting the Canadian automobile industry in some way, I could understand it. But in Canada today I think I am correct in saying there is little or no unemployment in the automobile industry. They are working at capacity, and you still cannot get a Chevrolet, Plymouth or a Ford without waiting for it. I believe there have been record sales for these cars-
Might I interrupt the hon. member to ask a question?
Yes.
Is the hon. member in the market for a Chevrolet? I have an excellent one.

I am talking about new cars, not second-hand ones. However, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian automobile industry today, I think I am correct in saying, can sell all the cars it can make. I suggest that Canadian consumers are having a difficult time paying the prices that some of these Canadian car manufacturers are demanding.

Customs Tariff
These English cars fill a place in the low price field, and I believe they are really needed. It the time comes later when these British cars-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: None of these low priced cars are paying any dumping duties now because the manufacturers have stopped dumping. They are coming in free.
Then why not leave the dumping duties the way they were?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend would like an answer to that now, I can give it. I thought I had made it clear that the dumping clause in the Canadian tariff is and has been for forty-five years a fundamental part of the tariff. Its purpose, and its sole purpose, is to prevent unfair competition. Any exporter in another country can send his products to Canada, and if he sends them here at a value which is not below the fair market value in the market in which they are produced the normal rates of duty apply or they come in free. There have been long discussions in this house in years past as to the very serious effect there may be upon Canadian domestic producers if people in foreign countries can dump their surplus production in Canada at prices which bear no relation to the value of the article.

Mr. Chairman, I accept the statement of the minister, but I still cannot agree with him. For many years I have listened to the Liberal party say that they believe in freer trade. The minister says, we are going to give you freer trade but we will have to have these dumping duties. It does not seem to me to be a consistent policy. I have heard the Minister of Finance tell the British car industry to get their prices down and become competitive, to produce a product that would sell on the Canadian market. Then he said they can earn dollars for England and in turn can buy your wheat and your farm products. It seems to me that the British automobile industry has done this, and the minute that they have got their prices down to that level, Canada goes and puts this dumping duty on. I say that this dumping duty is completely undesirable, that it is inconsistent with Liberal policy of freer trade, and that I think it should be put back in the same state as it was prior to May 31.

May I ask the minister if he can give us this information? Let us take the case of an Austin car which sells for around $1,400, I believe. Has there been any difference in the selling price at which that car was sold in Canada prior to the restoration of the dumping duties and the price at

which it sold in Canada after the restoration of the dumping duties? Can he give us a concrete example?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The actual situation is that the dumping duties are still suspended and will be suspended until the end of this month. But the export price of Austin cars, to which my hon. friend refers, to Canada, now is such that, if the dumping duties had not been suspended, it still would not make any difference because there would not be a dumping duty applicable. In other words, the export price of the particular car to which my hon. friend refers is a price which represents the fair market value in the United Kingdom; and I believe that has been the case ever since sterling was devalued.

Did the
minister not say that there was one exception to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that there is; but until the first of June I cannot prove that. I think that it will be found that in the case I mentioned-and perhaps I may mention the name

namely the Vauxhall car, which is a more expensive car, it is still being exported to Canada at a price which would attract a dumping duty if the dumping duty were still applicable.

On May 3, when this resolution was under discussion, I brought to the minister's attention the fact that the Americans were subsidizing apple exports to other countries at the rate of $1.25 per box. At that time I said that included Canada, but I was mistaken. I should have said that because of the large volume of exports going out of the United States, the greater volume of apples exported received a subsidy of $1.25 a box, which makes it possible for the United States exporters to dump apples into Canada at an extremely low price. The minister at that time said that he would have the situation checked. Has he any information to give us at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that my parliamentary assistant has some information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The Department of Agriculture and the Department of National Revenue looked into the situation and found out that the United States' subsidy is not paid on sales on the North American continent. The subsidy was mainly for ECA shipments and for assistance in getting rid of a large surplus of apples which the Americans had. There is an excellent statement on apple holdings in the Canadian Grower of April 23. I do not know that it is necessary to put it on record. But Canadian growers themselves feel that British Columbia apples in particular

are holding their own on this eastern market. It is the same problem as the Canadian growers have, because in the Okanagan valley there is a surplus of McIntosh Reds at the moment.
While I am on my feet, I might say that there are two small amendments-

If the parliamentary assistant will permit me to interrupt, may I say that I think that statement should not be allowed to go unamplified. The reason British Columbia apples held their own on eastern markets in recent months is that, in order to hold that market, the producers sold them at less than the normal price. They sold apples at $1 a box, I think it was; although it is true that they sold apples on this market, they had to sell them at the low price of $1 a box because of what amounted to a dumping duty by American producers.

And they are better
apples too.

I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley that they were better apples; and if it were not for dumping duties, subsidies or things like that, they could hold their own and win in any market in the world.
Hear, hear.

I think an important factor in this apple business is that British Columbia delivers her apples to one particular level in the United States market; and the removal of the lower price United States apples from the market has resulted every year in a sale by British Columbia-as it has since last year, of two and a third million boxes-at the highest price of any apples exported from British Columbia. They demand there an extremely high grade, particularly of Delicious, a few Winesaps, and some McIntosh Reds. They go principally to several acknowledged and long-time markets in the United States, like New Orleans. Prices as high as $3.55 a box, f.o.b. Okanagan, have been paid for those apples, -all extra fancies. The removal of the lower grades from the United States I think has kept that market open for our highest grades, longest-priced British Columbia apples.

customarily used in the manufacture of margarine, but I am afraid the Minister of Finance is not keeping up to date on what goes on in this city of Ottawa where they are trying to ruin the dairy farmers. Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance will remember that on May 3 I suggested an alternative source from which he could obtain revenue, and as reported on page 2637 of Hansard I presented tables to the committee showing the net profits after taxes, made by, the dividends paid by, and the undistributed profits remaining in the hands of Canadian corporations. At that time I was told that the proper time to discuss that whole matter would be on the income tax resolution.
My suggestion was ruled out of order at that time, so at this time I should like to ask the minister one or two things about this whole question. I think the minister believes that the government should arrange its taxes so that they will be collected more or less on the basis of ability to pay. I think I am correct in that assumption. If I am correct, then I should like to know whether the minister honestly believes that the new taxes he is proposing in his budget will be collected strictly on the basis of ability to pay. I would ask him if it would not be sensible to go to the place where the money is in order to get increased revenues.
If his answer is in the affirmative then I should like to have him answer another question. Is it not true that he could easily pbtain another $100 million from the undistributed profits of corporations? On May 3 Jl suggested that 1951 was not likely to be a worse year than 1950. I pointed out that in that year the net profits of corporations in Canada, after taxes, amounted to $1,402 million. The cash dividends distributed to Canadians and other individuals and corporations abroad amounted to $672 million. That left undistributed profits of $730 million. That was $129 million more than the undistributed profits in 1949, which was a good year. In that year the corporations paid quite substantial dividends of $570 million, which left in their possession undistributed profits of $601 million.
On May 3 I also pointed out that during the nine years from 1942 these corporations had accumulated undistributed profits to a total of $4,648 million. At that time I said that I was in favour of the profit motive
Income Tax Act
because I believe that a reasonable profit perhaps is the greatest inducement for production, the provision of services and that sort of thing. But when I see individuals of *this country being loaded with a 20 per cent income tax surcharge for defence needs; when I see them being faced with a 25 per cent increase in the sales tax; when I realize that they just have not in their possession accumulated savings from which to obtain these extra charges; when I realize that consumers of this country are having a terrible struggle to make ends meet under the impact of the highest cost of living in the history of this country; I wonder why it is there is so much indifference to the suggestion that the $100 million which the minister said he needs from the sales tax-I doubt it very much- could not be obtained by turning to the corporations and asking them during the next two or three years when profits might be expected to be buoyant that they pay, not a 20 per cent surcharge but a 40 per cent surcharge on their income tax.
I suggested on May 3 that by doing that he would obtain $100 million and yet would leave in their possession undistributed profits of not less than $500 million for 1951, which of course was calculated on the basis of 1950 performance. The minister's forecast pretty much substantiates what I said. I ask the minister if it would not be more fair to impose a 40 per cent surcharge this year on corporation profits, realizing that it would still leave them $500 million in undistributed profits, than to place this load on the taxpayers of this country in the form of an increased sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The first question asked by my hon. friend was whether we should not go to where the money is. Of course we should, if we are aiming solely at revenue, which is one of the major purposes of the budget. Then he asks if that is the case why we should not go and take a full share of undistributed profits. In my budget speech I tried to make it as clear as I could why I think that as a general rule, and except in very exceptional circumstances, it is a mistake to attempt to take 50 per cent or more of profits from any organization. I think it makes for waste and inefficiency. In fact with this 20 per cent surcharge, if one includes the provincial tax of 5 per cent in the concurring provinces and 7 per cent in Quebec and Ontario, we are over that 50 per cent.
I think it should be realized that the undistributed profits of corporations are not in fact in cash. They are invested as a rule in plant, equipment, inventory and so on. Actually over the past four or five years in particular that has been one of the major sources of the increase in our productive

Income Tax Act
resources, expansion of plant, equipment and so on. To answer my hon. friend's question directly, I believe that it would be most unfair to put a 40 per cent surcharge, as he has suggested, on corporation profits. After all, we have to remember that corporations are not individuals, and that those profits are taxed again when they ultimately get into the hands of the shareholders. In that sense it is double taxation and the corporation is only a vehicle for collecting taxes.
I think it should also be realized that under existing conditions taxes imposed on business concerns probably go into the price of the goods, and with demands as they are now I must say that my own view is that an excessively high corporation tax could provide an impetus to inflation. I do not know that I can add very much to that. One can argue indefinitely as to the merits and demerits of a particular tax, but the job a minister of finance always has is to try to spread the burden of the taxes which he has to impose as fairly as he can. That is what I have tried to do this year. At the same time I think he has to try to use taxes as a fiscal and economic weapon to check inflationary forces. That again is what I have endeavoured to do in this budget. As I have said before, I do not claim any monopoly on wisdom, but the budget this year does represent my best judgment as to how those two purposes can be accomplished, and it of course carried the judgment of my colleagues in the government.

Could the minister obtain figures which would indicate the portion of undistributed profits that were turned back into plant investment and expansion, and at the same time the percentage of undistributed profits that have found their way into unproductive investment such as bonds and securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am told that there are probably no figures which would enable that to be given accurately. You would have to look at the balance sheets of the various business enterprises of the country. There is a real incentive under existing conditions to reinvest earnings in plant and equipment rather than keep them in low yield bonds. Speaking generally, I think it is fair to say that by far the greater proportion of the undistributed earnings of the business enterprises of this country have been reinvested in plant and equipment, bricks and mortar, machinery and so on. That has been demonstrated time and time again when you come to examine the record of a family business, for instance, over a period of years. You will find that it starts from small beginnings and it is

largely built up by reinvested profits. I think that is probably pretty characteristic of the pattern in this country and in most other countries like ours.

I think that is perfectly true in connection with family corporations, but it would be very interesting to look at the investment portfolios of many of the corporations. I attempted to go into that whole matter and to find some figures that would be accurate, but as the minister says it is difficult.

A surplus in these small companies is certainly the lifeblood of them, and the reinvesting of part of it into the business, putting it back into increased plant. If, in the first year they start to produce anything, the minister takes half of it to start with-and if there are any profits at all, they are invested in the company-the minister has a preponderant interest in it. Rather than tax surplus itself, I think maybe the profits that are not distributed should be taxed at a lower rate than distributed profits, and when they are taken out of surplus again, perhaps the tax could be larger than 15 per cent; but the minister has already covered that.

What happens under that sort of arrangement is this. Profits are left in the hands of companies who reinvest them in capital equipment and otherwise. In reality, you are taking from the public funds by means of profits and reinvesting them. In other words, the prfblic are thus paying for the capital equipment; but the company owns the equipment and assets afterwards.
What I really rose to say to my hon. friend is this. There is one aspect of this problem that I think we are overlooking-it is one perhaps that concerns the present economic system rather more than it would a different system-and it is this. By means of this method, corporations are becoming independent of the savings of the great mass of the public, of the banks, of trust companies and of other financial institutions, with the 80709-200J

result that power in our economy is becoming concentrated more and more in the hands of a group of industrialists. What we are really witnessing to some extent is a transfer of power from financial institutions and investors who did a normal business and performed a normal function in our economy years ago, and a concentration of that power into the hands of another group in our society. At the same time, they are preventing what was quite common prior to this important change, namely the small investor finding a place where he can invest his savings and his funds. He is narrowed down more and more merely to government bonds and other types of low-interest securities.
He can go to the stock market.

My hon. friend says "Go to the stock market." He knows that the stock market is much more speculative than is the reinvestment of funds in the company which is controlled by directors who have at their disposal all the information that is necessary to decide whether the investment is likely to be worth while or not. The average man has to take a chance with the stock market. I am pointing that out because I think in the present development' of our economy it is something that needs to be considered. It does not matter what your point of view is politically; there, I think, is a new and important factor; and is one of the reasons why I suggest that a tax on undistributed profits would be a good tax in this new country with a developing industrial economy.

I feel that there is one point that the socialists have overlooked in this discussion, namely that the most important thing in the Dominion of Canada is full employment. Wages are only relative. It does not much matter whether a man earns $10 a day or $5 a day as long as the things that he buys are relative to his earnings. The minister s taxation policy on corporations is one means of creating full employment. Canada is growing, and we must have capital for our industries, if they are to grow too. This is one means of placing capital at the disposal of industries in a reasonable manner, thus creating employment. Anyone who is opposed to increasing industries is opposed to the creation of jobs for the people who live in Canada. Since our population is increasing it becomes more imperative than ever that we have more and more industries. I suggest therefore that any legislation such as this, which tends to create more jobs and to give more work to labourers and which tends to bring about the good times we are now enjoying, is sound legislation.
