Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to speak on this complex question, because there are so many different views which could be expressed-and I have not the benefit of experts to advise me. However, after observing over some years the result of policies put into effect on the advice of experts, I have come to the conclusion that the experts can be wrong, too. If we have been following the advice of experts, and if they are not wrong, then I wonder how we have got into the mess we are in now.
Some hon. members seem to have strange views on the methods of increasing taxes, or of raising revenue. Several times each day I listen to newscasts-indeed, that is about the only radio program in which I am interested. I have noticed that, for the last while, every time I turn on the radio an appeal is made to the young men of Canada, most of whom have no property at all, to help save our free way of life. And, Mr. Chairman, if one may judge from what is happening in Korea today, saving our way of life may involve something more than paying some of our surplus money in taxes. It may, and sometimes does, involve the supreme sacrifice of life itself.
It seems to me that if we are to ask people to pay taxes, particularly if taxes are of such proportion as to involve a sacrifice, they should be told the purpose of the sacrifice. For most people paying taxes is a sacrifice, because they do not understand the purpose for which they are paying the taxes. Indeed, we have never told our people clearly why we must tax heavily. The result is that people complain that they are not going to work just in order that Doug Abbott may have a little more money. I do not take that position, because I know it is not the correct one to take. It is not Doug Abbott who gets the money; he is just the collector. The money is for Canada, and for all its people.
The criterion as to whether our taxes are heavy or light is not how much we pay but how much we have left after the taxes are paid.
When one considers the corporations that have 50 per cent of their not inconsiderable profits left, and compares them with the ordinary citizens of Canada who have not only nothing left when they have paid their year's bills, but have not had enough income in the first place to give them a decent standard of living, one realizes at once who is making the sacrifice. We know then where we should seek the money. We should look for it where it is, and we should not be taking it from people who did not have it in the first place.

Let us not forget that, as applied to a large proportion of the people in Canada, every cent we take from them in sales tax or other taxes, direct or indirect has to be restored to them through social services of one kind or another. That is the case because they are not paid a sufficient amount for producing the wealth of this country to enable them to live decently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have to pay for the defence of the country, too.

Yes, we have to pay for the defence of the country. But in paying for defence consideration must be given to what one has to defend; and I say the corporations of Canada have much more to defend than have the ordinary men on the street who today may have jobs and who tomorrow are out of jobs.
Let us look at this picture as it is, and not try to talk about it from preconceived ideas that do not at all meet the situation we are dealing with today.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on this matter. There have been times in the house when a matter of this kind has been discussed with a good deal of seriousness. Lately however it has not been. The reason is that when anyone rises to criticize the government he feels, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, like the little boy who has spit in the cathedral.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do you feel like that?

The subject is almost sacred; one must not talk about it. "We have decided -and there are an awful lot of us." The opposition are hesitant, because those are the people who handle the payrolls and who give out the jobs. They are all-important.
That kind of thinking is out of date. Even in his day, Abraham Lincoln said, in respect of the question of capital versus labour, that labour created capital and wealth, and that labour came first, and that if it were not for labour there would be no capital. If I sit back and live off the swfeat of another man's brow, I am not the emancipator: the reverse is true. If it were not for the fact that there are thousands of men and women in Canada who are content with their humble role of producing the country's wealth for very little in return, a great many exalted persons who are making large sums of money would be starving, because they could not produce enough for themselves.
I do not say that disparagingly, because we recognize this as the scheme of things. What prompted me to rise at this time was the

remark of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, a very good friend of mine, and an old logger who went through the mill.
Broken down.
But finally his background has got away from him. He has gravitated down here and mixes among the exalted, so that he is beginning to forget where he came from.
I sit in opposition, too.

He said the hon. member for Kootenay West in moving his amendment had not defined what excess profits were. I would point out that that has been defined many times in the house. The government itself set the formula in 1940, 1941 and 1942 when it said, "If you were in business between 1936 and 1939 your normal profits will be struck in relation to those three years, and we will perhaps give you fifteen or twenty per cent more than that." Excess profits were considered at that time, and the provision worked out satisfactorily.
The fact of the matter is that most of the plant and equipment in Canada today was financed by the taxpayer and written off at accelerated depreciation. We do not own those goods; we gave it away; for three years we wrote it off. That is a very easy way of getting into business.
There would be no difficulty today in setting up an excess profits tax. The government could say, "We are going to go back to 1947, and make that your normal profit." There has been a skyrocketing of profits since 1947, as indicated by the table put on the record by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Do you want to allow him a little more on top of what he is getting today?
I think the hon. member for Vancouver East dealt with this quite properly. We are asking men to give up everything they have in this country to fight for us. Do not make any mistake about it, it is not the executives and the fellows who make the payrolls who are going to do the fighting in Korea or anywhere else. This fighting will be done by the man who works in the shop or the factory, the young fellow who is physically fit and who is making perhaps $2,000 per year. He is the one who is going to do the fighting; he is the one who has always done the fighting.
You are asking these fellows to put on uniforms to save the institutions of this country for as little as $2.35 per day, when they are swapping at least $10 or $12 per day in other occupations. He is asked in the final analysis to perhaps risk his life for $2.35 per day. In the face of the profits made today by large corporations across this country how
Income Tax Act
can anyone justify asking these young men to do that kind of job unless he is prepared to make similar sacrifices?
In my opinion inflation is the greatest enemy we have. It constitutes the most serious defence matter we have to consider. We are spending $5,000 million in the next three years, and on the basis of present prices we are going to get only half value; we are going to lose in purchasing power about 50 per cent of the money we will spend on defence. The Minister of Finance has said that we must pay for defence. Certainly we must, but who is getting that extra money because of inflation? It is no one else but the fellow who is marking that ledger and skyrocketing profits. There is no doubt about it, he is price fixing. He sets his own prices. He calls the shots. All this leads to waste and extravagance and that kind of thing.
If that analysis is correct, it adds up to simple dishonesty. I have never seen it that way. I think of the progress we have made in pensions and all that kind of thing in the last ten years and I suggest that it is all due to the fact that these corporations decided they might as well pay out profits in that way rather than in excess profits taxes. If we had good stiff excess profits taxes I think they would go a long way toward stopping rising prices. There would be no incentive to raise prices if you could not keep your profits.
I think this matter will have to be considered seriously. We are only just beginning to siphon off manpower and buy our defence equipment. I think that is one particular spot the government should get tough with. I think the time has come when we should all consider it most seriously. The fellow who makes the payroll should not think he is all-important. I consider that the fellow who produces the payroll is the important man. Without him there would be no payroll. The fellow who is just writing figures and making a good profit out of them should consider himself very lucky in comparison with the man who produces the wealth.
I know we cannot do anything about these matters. As I said a moment ago, we are just bumping our heads against a stone wall. But it does not do any harm to have a re-examination of conscience every once in a while in the hope that we might be able to drive home to the Minister of Finance and his advisers that this is one matter they will have to tackle, if for no other reason that for defence and the encouragement of those whom we are asking to leave home and go to other parts of the world to make great sacrifices for us.
I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni about the right to a profit on your investment. Sometime

Income Tax Act
he should go to the library and get the Macdonald report on the British Columbia mining industry. He will see where these rights were given away for the building of a railroad and then capitalized at about $10 million. They got these rights for nothing, they marked up the price of coal in order to pay dividends on watered stock of about $11 million, and around and around it went just like a merry-go-round. That report offers a pretty good analysis of practically every corporation in this country. When you squeeze all the water out of their stock they will not find it hard to pay profits on the actual capital invested.
I hope this discussion will be taken seriously by the minister and he will come into the house shortly and say that his conscience has bothered him a little and he believes this is necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I say that in my view the discussion could be more closely related to section 1. Certain statements were made, then the minister gave some explanations, but from there on the committee has got into an academic discussion covering the whole field of economics within and outside Canada. If the discussion does not terminate shortly by the clause carrying I feel that, for the benefit of hon. members who are not participating in the discussion, I shall have to intervene and indicate that the discussion must be relevant to the item before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that we all agree with your'observations and will want to abide by your ruling in respect to these matters. However, corporation taxes are somewhat involved. Speakers who have preceded me have attempted to draw a comparison between the justice of taxing the wage earner and those who produce the wealth and permitting corporations to pile up certain profits without similar taxation.
I should like to say a word to those who have preceded me. I think perhaps we are pursuing a wrong tack. Those who have spoken in this debate have spoken rather powerfully, but the minister has sat there without saying a word. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar referred to certain financial policies followed in Great Britain and the minister twigged a slight error that was not of great consequence and rase momentarily to point it out. However, he did not answer the argument. The hon. member who leads this group spoke rather powerfully, as did the hon. member for Vancouver East, and we have just listened to a plea for justice by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

May I say to these gentlemen that I think the tack we should follow in our pleading with the minister is to say to the minister: Mr. Minister, do you agree with that? Is the soldier in Korea paid so much today and does he have to pay taxes? Do you agree with that? Is that right? If the minister says it is right then it will go right into Hansard. We should follow the same course right through because I can see that all the pleadings we may make with the very passions that flow from the innermost parts of our souls are not going to change the minister's mind. The hon. member for Cape Breton South hopes that the minister's conscience may prick him so that he will return later and reverse his policy. My, my, what a hope! Finance ministers come and finance ministers go, but the financial policy remains the same. Therefore I think, gentlemen, that we will have to go into a huddle and change our tactics to see if we cannot prick the minister's conscience enough for him to say right now: You have got me there, boys. I cannot keep back the tears. I must change this policy right away.
May I ask the minister whether any further consideration has been given to relieving the active service forces from having to pay income tax while they are on active service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I intend to deal with that at some length when we come to the section dealing with amendments to the income tax relating to the armed forces.
Mr. Chairman, most of the talking seems to be taking place on this opposition side of the house tonight, and I think I may as well get in a word or two for half a minute.
You had better be careful.

One of the hon. members on my left stated that the public is paying, so far as these corporations are concerned. I should like to tell him that, so far as the government of Great Britain to which he referred is concerned, I think the people of Great Britain are paying. If I had known this discussion was coming up tonight I would have brought with me a letter that I received from a relative in Great Britain about three weeks ago, and I would have read it on this occasion. Another hon. member mentioned the mess we find ourselves in. I think there are many people in other countries of the world, which have a different system from our own, who are also finding themselves in a mess. While the socialists' idea is that they will get social security and economic freedom through

a system different from ours, I think they will find that in the final analysis they will end up with no social security or economic freedom. I contend these are things that we should keep in mind when we are discussing this issue tonight.

I should like to take a minute or two to say something in this debate. I had not intended to, but after hearing the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Kootenay West I thought I should make my own position clear. In this party we can differ now and then, and I regret that I must say that I do differ tonight with some of the views that have been expressed by members of my own party. The corporation tax level in Canada and in my own province of Saskatchewan is now 51 per cent. I have a small business, and perhaps I am biased because of that. Nevertheless when I pay that 51 per cent I pay it in hard cash and the minister leaves me my stock in trade and bad debts, many of which may or may not be collected. I think that he is taking a lot more than 51 per cent from me at the present tax levels.
I also believe that when he stated that in England only 10 per cent of undistributed profits are taxed he had a very strong point. I could be all wrong but it seems to me that, so far as taxes on corporations in Canada are concerned, we have almost reached the saturation point in peacetime. If war comes of course a further excess profits tax may possibly be imposed; but at the present time, and speaking from my own experience, I do not think that taxes can go very much higher. I say that to make my own position clear. If more revenue is needed then I think it is going to have to come from greater production, perhaps from more people in the country or something of that kind. Perhaps we are even going to have to borrow if we need more money for defence. As I say, I could be all wrong but I do not think my colleagues will object to my making my position clear.

One of the great strengths
of democratic organizations is of course that there can be differences of opinion expressed freely and openly.

Hang on to the good
ones.

I certainly do not deplore
that sort of thing. I want to say, however, that I think my hon. friend is mistaken in one particular at least. This is not peacetime. What we are suggesting is a policy that in reality is a wartime policy. It is true that we are not engaged in the kind of war in which we were involved from 1939 to 1945, but we are spending as much money this year as we did in the early part of that
Income Tax Act
great struggle. To that extent, while it is a defence effort, it is analogous in expenditure to a war effort. I am also going to say that I suggested when I rose a little earlier that we should have a graduated tax on corporations, as we have on individuals. The Minister of Finance pointed out that there was a certain exemption now for the smaller corporations. That is true, and I think that can be adequately defended, but what we are pointing out in our remarks tonight is that here we see these vast accumulations of money. It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that it is not in liquid form and therefore no part of it could be paid in taxes, but that is not wholly true. A great deal of it is in liquid form. It comes into their hands in liquid form. It can remain in liquid form, and it can be liquidated by the Minister of Finance.
I believe that we are expressing a point of view that is sound, just and fair. The hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out very accurately and forcefully that we are asking thousands of young Canadians to offer to surrender not their profits but their lives, and when they do not surrender their lives, they risk their futures, for the defence of the democratic way of life which, regardless of our political views, we all profess and wish to defend. I do not want to transgress the rules, Mr. Chairman, but I want to say that I believe we are speaking, not only for our party but for a large number of people who are not of our party, when I say that instead of taxing the less fortunate individual, who is finding it very difficult indeed to get even the necessaries of life, we should call upon those who have accumulated vast amounts of wealth and of power to surrender, in this time of preparation for defence and high expenditures, some of that wealth and thereby relieve the people of this country from the great burdens that they have to carry.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise to protest against the application of this 20 per cent surtax to individuals at the low level to which it is made to apply. We have already expressed our opposition in the form of a subamendment during the main budget debate, but I repeat that we feel it is most unfair that married couples with less than $3,000 of income should be called upon to pay this 20 per cent surtax.
We all recognize the need to increase the income tax rates if additional revenue must be found. Indeed, when we were discussing the resolution having to do with commodity taxes we objected to taxes of that kind on the ground that they are not based on ability to pay. We argued that the fairer tax to employ is the income tax, because it is based on ability to pay. Therefore we assert that when larger revenues are required the proper kind of taxes to employ include a graduated corporation tax and a graduated personal income tax.
We contend, however, that you destroy the whole principle of graduating those taxes, and you defeat the aim of basing them on ability to pay, when you apply this 20 per cent increase right across the board starting with the very first dollar of income tax a person has to pay. At the present time the exemption levels are $1,000 in the case of a single person and $2,000 in the case of a married person. This means that a married couple without children, with an income of $3,000, have an exemption of $2,000 and pay income tax on $1,000. The amount of tax

paid under the old rates was $150. This surtax will require that couple to pay an additional tax of $30. I point out that back in the period 1935 to 1939, when the dominion bureau of statistics worked out the cost of living index to which we make frequent reference, the income tax exemption level under the federal act was $2,000, just the same as it is now. In addition to that the allowance for a dependent child was $400 as opposed to $150 at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. That is what the hon. member is trying to do. I was endeavouring to point out that during the years 1935 to 1939 when the cost of living index was worked out at 100, it was on the basis that the actual expenditure incurred by certain so-called average families amounted to $1,453 a year. When we talk of today's cost of living index being 181-8, it means that it costs 181-8 per cent of that $1,453 for that same basket of goods and services. Now I point out that when the recognized basket of goods and services cost $1,453 a year the income tax exemption for a married couple was $2,000. Today that same basket of goods and services costs well over $2,600, yet the income tax exemption level is still the same figure of $2,000.
If it were peacetime, today's high cost of living would make our case unanswerable that the exemption level for a married couple

Income Tax Act
should be raised to $3,000 with comparable increases for children. I insist on that; if it were not for the wartime or semiwartime conditions facing us, today's cost of living would make it essential that there be no income tax below the $3,000 level. In view of the situation we are in and the need for additional revenues, I suggest the least the minister should do is exempt those people with incomes between $2,000 and $3,000 from this surtax. The same argument applies with respect to single persons. Their exemption at the moment is $1,000. I should say that certainly the first $500 of their taxable income -the amount from $1,000 to $1,500-should not be subject to this 20 per cent surtax.
It would be very easy to work that out in the form of an amendment if there were any possibility of persuading Your Honour that an amendment would be in order. I recognize all the rulings that were made during the other debate, however, and I will not put Your Honour to the trouble of looking up the book to find ways in which to rule out of order any amendment I might make, but I will suggest the kind of amendments which it seems to me would be appropriate. Perhaps if I suggest them to the minister and leave him the privilege, he may move one himself. On the one hand it could be proposed that there be an amendment to paragraph 2 adding a phrase similar in spirit to the last part of paragraph 1. We remember that paragraph 1 had a qualifying clause to the effect that the surtax was not to reduce the income of a corporation below a certain point. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance, since he could move the amendment although I could not because it would be a money amendment, to add to clause 2 an amendment which would suggest that these taxes are subject to the right of refund where they reduce the net income of the taxpayer to a point below that necessary to maintain a decent standard of living at today's prices. Is that not just as fair a request as was contained in the qualifying clause with respect to paragraph 1? The minister wants to get additional revenue out of corporations. He wants to get all that he can but he wants to be fair. He must not go too low, so he puts in a qualifying phrase. The minister wants to get all the money he can out of the personal income tax. Why should he not be fair to the single person in the $1,000 to $1,500 bracket, and to married couples between $2,000 and $3,000, and add a qualifying phrase such as the one I have suggested based on the kind of qualifying phrase he put in paragraph 1?
If that sort of amendment seems rather hard for the minister to word in such a way as to define the amount necessary to maintain a decent standard of living, then he could do it very simply by means of another amendment which I would offer to him. It would read something like this: That this surtax set out in paragraph 2 shall not apply to the first $150 of tax paid by a married couple or to the first $75 of tax paid by a single person. That is a simple way to do it, and it achieves the proposal that we made in our subamendment during the course of the budget debate. The figure of $150 is the amount of tax paid under the present rate by a married couple on their first $1,000, that is the $1,000 between the figures of $2,000 and $3,000. I suggest that bracket should not be subject to surtax. In other words, the first $150 of tax paid by a married couple should not be subject to this 20 per cent. Similarly, in the case of a single person the first $75 paid is, to use the same kind of example, the tax he pays on the amount between $1,000 and $1,500; in other words, the first $500 of taxable income. There, too, I suggest that the surtax should not be paid.
I recognize, Mr. Chairman, that this proposal was made in our budget subamendment, but it was not discussed to any great extent during the course of the budget debate. I do not recall the minister replying to it. I feel that he should now deal with this matter, and indicate whether or not it is possible to give consideration to this suggestion. He brought down his budget on April 10, and at that time we had before us a cost of living index figure which was the highest in history. Another month end has gone by and that highest figure in history has gone still higher. I point out that this simply means that single persons with less than $1,500 income and married persons with less than $3,000 a year income are finding it still harder to make both ends meet. I believe it is a most reasonable request, namely, that the people in those brackets should not be subject to this defence surtax.
I wish to make it clear that I am not opposing the main part of paragraph 2. When we were discussing the sales tax we said that the income tax was a fairer method. Now that we are on the income tax, I support it. If it is necessary to make up for any loss of revenue because of my proposal that these lower income groups be not subject to the surtax, that could be made up in either one of two ways: either by increasing the percentage in the higher brackets or by going back to paragraph 1 and increasing the rates in the upper brackets of corporation income tax. Like the member for Macleod, Mr. Chairman, I hope that when we are

Income Tax Act
making these proposals we are not just pouring out our hearts and making an impassioned plea which the minister is going to ignore. I am sure he will not. I am sure he will discuss this matter, and that he will find there is a pretty general feeling amongst members in all parties that it is unfair to impose this surtax at the low levels which this paragraph proposes it should apply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to comply with my hon. friend's request and deal with his suggestion. There are two elements in connection with the imposition of any personal income tax; one is the level of exemptions and the other is the rate at which the tax is imposed. As is well known to all members of the house, our exemptions are very much higher than the exemptions in the United Kingdom, and higher than the exemptions in the United States. The tax that is imposed, even with the surtax which is now suggested, on the people in the group to which my hon. friend has referred, the $3,000 group and below, is infinitely less than the tax which is imposed in the United Kingdom, and very much less than the tax that is imposed in the United States. I take these two countries as being countries whose responsibilities for defence and other things are, to some extent, comparable with our own.
Now, it is perhaps unnecessary for me to say that in formulating my tax proposals I gave most earnest consideration as to what should be done with respect to exemptions and what should be done with respect to the rates. I came to the conclusion, as I said in my budget speech, that for this year I did not propose to touch the exemptions, and I did not propose to touch the graduated rate schedule. But I did propose to put a twenty per cent surtax on the amount of the tax payable. Now, that represented the best judgment I could come to as the fairest way of spreading this burden, after a great deal of consideration and a good deal of discussion with my advisers. My colleagues agreed with my recommendations. It would be pleasant if we could get all the money we needed from people with incomes of $5,000, $6,000 or $7,000 per year or more, but there are not enough of them in the country to provide us with all the revenue. I suggest to the committee that since our exemptions are already higher than those two countries I mentioned, since the actual tax which is imposed even after the increase which I am suggesting is still substantially lower than the countries to which I have referred, it is rather difficult to suggest that this is a manifestly unfair tax schedule.

I should like to ask the
minister what the intent is under clause 2 (b)

with respect to the imposition of the surtax. Does this mean that the surtax will be calculated on what is described in the income tax form as net tax payable, or is it to be imposed before the allowance for the ten per cent dividends from taxable Canadian companies which is deducted from the tax? In other words, is it to be imposed on what is described in the income tax form as the total tax or is it to be imposed on what is described as the net tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The surcharge will be imposed on the tax as calculated before any tax credits are taken. Of course, in arriving at the income taxable one will deduct charitable donations, medical expenses and the like. Then a calculation will be made of the amount of tax. We have all been doing that for some time. The surcharge will apply to that figure. Then, when the tax payable is arrived at these credits will be taken for foreign taxes payable and so on.

On the tax form the ten
per cent of net dividends from taxable Canadian corporations is not described as a credit. What is described as a credit is a credit for foreign tax. The 10 per cent, as I understand it, was allowed to correct a practice which had been common in the department in former years which amounted to double taxation. By the allowance of this 10 per cent deduction it was felt that this practice had been at least partially overcome. If it is the intentiorj of the minister to revert to the former practice and permit this 20 per cent surcharge on the tax before allowance for dividends, then in effect what you are doing is going back to the former system and permitting at least some of this taxation in a double capacity. Twenty per cent of it, of course, would be double taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is merely a simple way of
calculation. Instead of changing the rate structure, we make a 20 per cent increase. It is merely a method of calculating your tax. There is no double taxation involved. I think my hon. friend is mistaken there.

No. The only mistake I
made is in not making myself clear, I am sure. I am thinking in particular of those people who have a small income almost entirely from dividends, from their savings. A great many of them were released from the obligation of paying taxes by reason of this allowance of 10 per cent against their taxes. Under this scheme, if it was a matter of $2,000, it means a difference of $40 tax to them, if the surtax is going to be imposed before the credit is allowed for the 10 per cent off Canadian dividends.

I think the suggestion made by
the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has a great deal of merit.
It is quite simple, too.

Yes, it is quite simple. But I
also think that the technique suggested by my colleague the hon. member for Macleod is a good one. In view of the fact that the Canadian dollar today is worth only about 55 cents in terms of the 1935-39 dollar, and consequently the $2,000 exemption for married people under the Income Tax Act would be worth only about $1,100, I am going to ask the minister if he does not think that the suggestion made by my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is sound. Does the minister not think that the individual taxpayer throughout this country ought to be given some consideration in virtue of the fact that his exemption today is not $2,000 but is actually $1,100? I am speaking of the married exemption. I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will answer my hon. friend's question in the negative. Since the $2,000 exemption before the war, we have fought a war and we have increased our debt some two or three times. We have all the additional charges imposed on Canadians as a result of the war. We have had a $400 million or $500 million addition to our social security payments. We must therefore raise more money from the taxpayers of this country.
As I said in reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, there are two elements to be considered in determining taxation. One is the rate of exemption and the other is the rate of the tax. Actually, the $3,000 married man with no dependents, to whom my hon. friend referred in his speech, paid $584 in taxes at the peak of war taxation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The cost of living index

181-8.

This year he will pay $150,
plus 10 per cent surtax or $15, a total of $165. It is all very well to talk about increasing the exemption and lowering the rate. But let me reiterate-as I have had to do so many times before-that one must get the money from the Canadian people, and one must get it from the people who earn

In reply to what the Minister

Has my hon. friend been in

On this point which has just been discussed, I should like to ask the minister whether the rates that he quoted-and he takes the years 1942 and 1943

include compulsory savings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. That was pure tax. '
To revert to my former question, I am still not clear whether the minister meant definitely that this surcharge would apply on the total tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me make it asi clear as I can. It is merely a method of calculating the tax. Suppose a person has a net taxable income of $1,000. His tax would be $150. Ten per cent added to that will make it $165. That is his tax payable. It could be done in another way. Instead of a 15 per cent rate, we could have made it an 18 per cent

Income Tax Act
rate. With half the rate for this year, you would have got exactly the same result. That is the tax.
There is a variety of tax credits. The taxpayers can take credit for 10 per cent of the dividends received from common shares; and if they have received $1,000 in dividends from common shares, they can deduct $100 from that $165 tax, just as they could last year; and if they have paid certain taxes in a foreign jurisdiction, I suppose they could deduct those. There is no change in principle or practice at all. It is merely a method of calculating the additional tax. If this system prevails throughout next year you could, I suppose, with equal force say that the initial rate would be 18 per cent instead of the 20 per cent surcharge. That is as clearly as I can explain it.

It is quite clear now. I was hoping that was not the case because, of course, as to those people who make just barely enough to get by, and when what they do make is the result of lifetime savings, it seems to me a great pity that they shall have to pay, the first full-year, an additional $40. It is lifting them out of the non-taxable class and putting them into the taxable class.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They could not have done that; because after all, there has been at least a 15 per cent rate on all income and the tax credit is 10 per cent.
If they made $1,500 in dividends, they would have $150 exemption which is the equivalent of the total tax they Would pay. If their income was $2,000, you can see where it places them.

I agree in great measure with what the minister has said. In fact, I can hardly understand how he is going to raise this large amount of money without the taxes that he is imposing. I tried to follow the arguments of my hon. friends to the left of me; but I do not think there is enough money in the big corporations for the government to be able to take from them sufficient to raise the money that is needed here for a war effort.
That, again, is only my opinion, of course. But there is one part of the population which I feel has suffered a great injustice, and I am referring to those who are on fixed pensions. I am sure the minister has taken this into consideration, but I should like to have an explanation of how, with the cost of living

index as it is today, a person on a pension fixed five or ten years ago can live in a normal fashion. I do not mean "normal" under present circumstances, but normal as we would expect he should be able to live. I do feel that in respect of fixed pensioners there is a great injustice, and that there should be a higher exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is the $500 exemption for those of sixty-five years and over, which includes a good many pensioners.
Many people on fixed pensions are not sixty-five years, but they still have to eat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is considered the normal pension age.
In other words they have to do the best they can until they reach the age of sixty-five. I think that is unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One would expect, unless they are incapacitated, that they would work until the age of sixty-five is reached.

In the discussion on paragraph 1 the minister established a precedent for doing exactly what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is asking him to do in connection with paragraph 2. The corporation making $10,000 or less in profits is not subject to the 20 per cent surtax. They pay only 15 per cent on their corporation tax, and do not come under this section at all. The precedent has been established whereby the small corporation does not have to pay the surtax. I do not see why the minister is not prepared to say that the man or woman on a small income should not be relieved from the 20 per cent surtax, inasmuch as the small corporations do not have to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot add anything to what I said a moment ago.
I wonder if the minister would mind telling us whether he is imposing these surtaxes or surcharges as an antiinflationary measure, or purely as a means of raising revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I made it clear in my budget speech that both elements were important. I need these moneys, both as a means of raising revenue and for the antiinflationary effect which, I believe, will be the result from the raising of the tax. That is my view. It may be a mistaken one.
Does the minister assume there is a shortage of supply of the ordinary necessities of life in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member's question covers a wide field. I would say there is a shortage of a good many essential materials,

such as steel, which enter into the production of the normal necessities people have to have. I think it is fair to say that there is today in Canada a greater supply of spending power than there is of immediately available goods. That is a major reason for the present inflationary tendencies. But if one includes in necessities of life basic food products, probably not, although apparently we have not an over-supply of butter at the present time.
Has the minister any statistics or figures by which he can establish that there is a relative shortage of goods as related to the money in actual working circulation in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think I have. I believe one has to draw that conclusion from the cost of living index.

I wonder if the minister is justified in drawing that conclusion from the cost of living index, having in mind the fact that the cost of living has risen largely as the result of manipulation rather than as the result of spending power.
Just to refresh the minister's mind along this line, may I recall to him that in April of 1946 the government granted the steel companies of Canada the privilege of advancing the price of steel by $5 a ton. I think the minister would have a hard time establishing, even before his most sympathetic friends, that that increase of $5 a ton was because people were buying more steel than was available in Canada. That $5 a ton increase was actually just a gift to the steel companies. And that $5 a ton increase in the cost of steel increased the cost of production, to which the minister referred a moment ago, and thereby it actually forced up the prices of commodities in Canada.
Then the minister will recall that, following the increase in price, there was a strike of the steel workers. They demanded that they be given their share of that $5 a ton. The result of the strike was that there was a substantial increase in the wages of the workers which, again, raised the cost of production of all commodities.
Now, can the minister honestly say that these two increases in the cost of production were the result of a shortage of goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I recall the incident to which my hon. friend refers, but it was in 1946, in the period of post-war inflation. I would hope that we might not have to enter into an extended discussion of inflationary forces of that time when we have before us this resolution relating to personal income tax. There was another debate on that subject earlier in the session, which arose from an
Income Tax Act
amendment to a motion to go into supply. At that time the cost of living was discussed. I can only say that what I have expressed represents the opinion I genuinely hold. I am quite prepared to concede, of course, that others may hold a different view; but I cannot give a more specific answer than that.

The point is that people in the House of Commons should come to grips with the problem of inflation, and not talk in generalities. There are many assumptions in the minister's position which, in my judgment, cannot be substantiated by the facts.
The whole question as to the validity of this impost, so far as it is looked upon as an anti-inflationary measure, depends upon whether or not there is actually in Canada a shortage of goods in reference to the amount of working purchasing power. There is no doubt about that. If that is so, then there could not be anything more pertinent to the question than this very discussion of inflation. It would be quite impossible to have anything more pertinent or more relevant than that. I believe the minister would agree on that point.
Then I would ask the minister this, simply because the people of Canada deserve to have an answer: If it could be found that there is a surplus of goods in Canada over what there was six months ago, then would it not be feasible and sound to create money and to spend it into circulation

because that money would not cause any increase in price.
I do not propose to enter into a discussion of that matter tonight, but I do believe that before the discussion of these budget resolutions is concluded the minister ought to attempt to show the House of Commons that he is justified in these outrageous imposts. He can say the people in Great Britain are being heavily taxed and that the people in the United States are being heavily taxed but that is no reason why the Canadian people should be so taxed, unless the situation in Canada justifies it.
If production in Canada is such that we can create money, instead of demanding it from the people-
The wrong time.

Never mind whether it is the wrong time or not. With you it is always the wrong time to discuss these matters. It is always the wrong time with the hon. member, because he cannot answer this argument, and the minister cannot answer it.

I know more about your
theory than you give me credit for.

If you know anything
about it, then get up and show it, and we will find out then what you know.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I had to deal with this young chap over here. There are a lot of people who think they know a lot until they are asked to prove it. If it is possible because of our large production to create that money then obviously these taxes are not necessary. Time and again we have heard it admitted that we could get revenue from increased production. If we have increased production, why cannot we get the revenue without taking it out of the pockets of the people?
In fairness to himself I think the minister ought to furnish statistics to establish the validity of the position he has taken. I maintain that the minister cannot show that the increases in prices which have resulted in this thing we call inflation are the result of surplus money in circulation. They are the result of direct and deliberate manipulation. I mentioned before how the price of steel was manipulated. These men simply 6aid that they were going to raise the price of steel $5 per ton. They did not care whether people needed steel. They did that and the government agreed with them and ever since then the people have been paying the shot. There is no question about that. That thing has pyramided until I wager it would be astonishing if the minister got the actual figures to show just how much the people of Canada have lost because of that increase of $5 per ton in steel. Until he is able to do so and until my brilliant young friend over here is able to do that I think it would be just as well for them to reserve judgment.
I do not think I shall say anything more about this. In the light of what I have said tonight I hope the minister will not say that this discussion is not relevant.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say a word
as to why this was done. As my hon. friend has said, he has been most assiduous in urging this on the government for a number of years. However, I know he will forgive me when I say he was not the first one that raised it. It has been urged for many years in the past.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Certainly; it was even in
the Income Tax Act in 1945.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The position with respect to union dues and a number of other things was this: The information which my predecessor got during the war was that the only deductions which were allowed from salaries and wages were some allowances for the running trades who were on a mileage basis. That was then extended to include all railway employees of. the running trades. My hon. friend is familiar with that. It was then extended to clergymen. My information up to the last two or three weeks was that those were the only deductions allowed. I was somewhat surprised to be informed by officials of the Department of National Revenue that in that respect I had been mistaken, and they too had apparently been mistaken. We found that in some parts of the country certain other allowances had been made. I think probably the hon. member for Cape Breton South will know for example that certain miners were allowed to deduct the expense of explosives they were using when they were on a piece work basis, and so on. There were some similar deductions of that kind.
I felt that if that was the case, and if it could be administered, it should be continued. Having arrived at the point where we were going to go into that field of deductions, I came to the conclusion that union dues should be given the same treatment. It is for that reason that they are included in the resolution now before the house. There

Income Tax Act
will be a definition in the bill as to what constitutes union dues. It will include the fees paid by civil servants to associations which are formed for the purpose of promoting better conditions of work and employment. They might not come technically within the ordinary understanding of union dues, but I hope it will be found that there is a clear definition of what constitutes union dues when the bill is brought before the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could the minister give any further details as to that definition now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would prefer not to do so. I think it would be better for the committee to have the definition before it. It will be seen that they are all directly related to the contract or work which is being performed.

There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister. First of all, I am asked this question with respect to subparagraph (e), which the minister has just been discussing, and I should like to put it on the record and ask to have it answered. I should like to know whether this includes the amount of pension assessments which are necessary or compulsory for union members to retain their membership standing.

speechtext: I will answer that part, but I would prefer to have the detailed discussion of this matter when we have the section before us. Pension assessments as such will not ' be included in this item because they are deductible under another provision in the act having to do with approved pension plans. Therefore pension contributions as such will not be eligible for deduction under this section. However, I would suggest to the committee, if it meets with their approval, that the detailed discussion as to what union dues will include should await the discussion of the definition itself. I will be ready to listen to any suggestion that may be appropriate to make it a clear definition.

Does the
phrase "contract of employment" imply a written contract?

speechtext: No, contract in the legal sense.

Just a working arrangement. Another matter which has been brought specially to my attention is [Mr. Abbott.l
the position of actors. I am told in a letter from one of them that they are not given the same status in Canada as they are in the United States and Great Britain. He says in part:
