speechtext: That's good.

If the minister has any difficulty in arriving at a definition I shall be glad to help him. I am not going to pursue that matter any further but will wait for the

bill. However, there are two matters of exemption that I should like to mention while we are dealing with exemptions because there is no other place to do it. The first one-and the minister himself brought it to my attention-is the question of miners, particularly those working underground, who have to purchase safety clothes such as shoes, a certain type of safety hat, and explosives. Explosives are not exempt for taxation purposes at this time. The minister might take that into consideration because practically everyone in a business in this country is permitted to deduct the legitimate expenses of operating that business. I think a man who has to buy shoes, a hat and explosives, which run into quite a bit of money a year, for the purpose of earning his income, should be permitted to deduct their cost for taxation purposes.
The second point I want to bring to the minister's attention is one about which the Department of National Revenue is a bit confused. I brought it to the department's attention on two or three occasions, and I got a mixed-up decision. I am not blaming them for that because perhaps this type of exemption of medical expenses applies to only one part of the country. The Department of National Revenue confused it with regular medical associations that collect from the individual and then pay his expenses for hospital and doctor. In the type of medical organization I have in mind that is not done. For example, the coal miners of Nova Scotia pay a doctor a dollar a week or $52 a year each as insurance. The doctor only supplies an examination and prescription. The individual pays for his medicine. The doctor keeps that money and pays nothing out of it. The type of service he gives is to diagnose your trouble and prescribe medicine.
In the second place the individual pays $52 a year to a hospital on a subscription basis. For that he gets ward treatment and ordinary services. I have brought two or three cases to the attention of the Department of National Revenue. The person affected, whose income was under $3,000 a year, had some $400 odd in medical expenses that year, minus this $104 by way of insurance, and he wanted to put in that $104 which he had paid the doctor and hospital on that subscription basis with his over-all hospital bill to make up the 4 per cent of his net income as an exemption for medical purposes. I know that whoever answered my letters confused that payment he made with payments made to associations that operate across the country and pay all medical bills. There is nothing paid back out of that $104, however. When
Income Tax Act
the minister is reviewing this matter of exemptions I hope he will take these questions into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not take time to deal with them tonight, but I will consider the points my hon. friend has raised.

I approve of the provision including union dues among the amounts which may be deducted for income tax purposes. The minister has now said that the definition will include fees to civil service associations, even though technically they may not be trade unions, and I am all for that. Before the minister draws up the final definition, however, I would like him to consider whether it might not also cover, as I think it should, the dues paid to farmers' unions and other farm organizations. It seems to me that if we are going to make this provision for professional people, for trade unionists and for civil servants, the same provision should be made for farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My understanding is that the farmer is a businessman, self-employed. This has reference to people on salaries and wages. However, I will make a note of that and be prepared to deal with it when we are discussing the section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In that case will the farmer be able to deduct those payments as an expense, as has been the case right along with doctors and lawyers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer that offhand. If it is a trade association I should think he would be able to do so. I have never even considered the position.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Paragraph agreed to.
4. That the governor in council be authorized to make regulations under which the income tax of members of the armed forces on their service income will be paid in full in respect of the pay and allowances of each pay period by a deduction therefrom in accordance with a special table subject to the right of any member to file a return on an annual basis.

What happens in the case of a man whose total income would not be taxable? Let me give the example of a university student who goes to camp for the summer, and who otherwise would not have any deductions. Will deductions be made monthly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that is provided for in the table. I had hoped to take a little time on this resolution to put before the committee some considerations in connection with the complete exemption from taxation of those serving in foreign theatres. Perhaps it would be equally convenient if I were to do that on the bill. I want to review our experience.

Income Tax Act
I am sure many hon. members here, particularly the hon. member for Nanaimo, are familiar with some of the difficulties we ran into during the last war. I should like to deal with them, to outline what we did and the problems we had to face, but I think perhaps I should not attempt to do that on this resolution this evening.
This is a proposal for a very simplified form of tax collection from the armed forces, where a table will provide for complete deduction. They will not be required to file a return if they do not have income in excess of $50 beyond their service pay. There will be an. allowance of $50 in lieu of charitable donations and so on; but it will be always open to the serviceman to file a return if it is more beneficial to him to do so. Of course the serviceman who is comparatively wealthy, who has an income in addition to his service pay, will be required to file a return and of course will get credit for the deductions made. My people tell me this new system has received the wholehearted endorsation of the national defence department. They believe it is a forward step over what we have had in connection with tax collection in previous, times, and I think it is an excellent system.
When we are considering the section of the bill I should like to say a word on the general question of the taxation of our armed forces. That is something about which I know a good deal, since Mr. Ilsley had me spend a good deal of time on it during the last war. I should like to put before the committee some facts with relation to it; in view of the late hour I would prefer not to do that tonight.
I point out to the minister that this question is of the utmost importance and also of the utmost interest to people from coast to coast in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree.

Many newspapers of all political stripes have taken very strong stands with regard to the taxation of men who are fighting in Korea. I believe the conscience of the Canadian people is very much troubled over this suggestion that the men who are doing the fighting in Korea are going to have to pay income tax. I hope the minister has changed his mind and that these men are not going to be taxed; but I am afraid we cannot wait until the bill is brought in to find out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be an excellent idea for me to deal with it tonight, then.

I would suggest that the
minister tell us now just what he is proposing with respect to the taxation of Canadians fighting in Korea.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps that is a good suggestion, and I will be happy to do so. The subject, as I say, is one with which I had a good deal of experience during the last war. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Royal the other day, such income tax exemption as has been suggested is very much more beneficial to the more highly paid officers than to the men. In the case of officers of the rank of general or higher it may be worth $140 a month or more. In the case of the other ranks it may be a few dollars a month at most.
The isubject had considerable attention during the last war. The three main headings under which I would like to discuss it are: first, the inequities and anomalies created within the services by tax exemptions granted in world war II; second, the inequities and anomalies created in relation to the rest of the taxpayers by the armed forces exemption; and third, the difficult administrative problems encountered in carrying into effect the armed services tax provisions in world war II. As hon. members know, in the United Kingdom armed services there is no such tax exemption and never has been.
Under the first heading, the inequities and anomalies created within the services by the tax exemptions we had in world war II, here is the history. We started out by granting an exemption for the ranks and leaving the officers to pay the full tax. That had the troublesome result, of course, that the higher levels of non-commissioned officers were receiving perhaps several hundred dollars more net income than the lowest levels of commissioned officers. Under those conditions it was understandable that warrant officers, for example, would be unwilling to take out commissions. The second step was the rectification of this anomaly by granting an exemption based on income. Any single member of the armed forces with an income of less than $1,600 was exempt, and married members were exempt at higher amounts. In addition a complicated tax credit formula was employed to gradually increase the tax above those exemptions until the full rate of tax was paid. At the same time a complete exemption for servicemen overseas was granted.
The fact that some servicemen in Canada were required to pay tax created considerable resentment. This group felt that it was a condition of their enlistment that they be required to perform their duties anywhere, and it was not of their own choice that they

happened to be stationed in Canada. I know from personal experience that there was a very real sense of grievance among those groups. Many officers, of course, whose services were required here, would far rather have been engaged in active duty at the front, and they felt that the imposition of income tax upon them completely disregarded that circumstance.
In the third place the position of one group of officers in Canada, who would otherwise have been taxable, was recognized by the granting of an exemption. These were the personnel of the services whose duties were normally performed either in the air or afloat. In the practical administration of that test, as I am sure a good many service members of the house will recall, it was necessary to adopt some simple rule as to eligibility. Unfortunately once a specific test had been adopted the temptation was presented to qualify for income tax exemption by meeting the requirements of the test. In short, it became possible to fly or float into a tax-exempt position, and of course it was impossible to establish any system for determining whether or not the exemption had been really earned. I might add that the possibility of obtaining complete exemption by a stint of duty overseas was also one that presented a constant temptation. I found, in my own brief experience in national defence, that there was a certain tendency to post people overseas in order to give them tax exemption, although they may never have got very much further than headquarters in London.
In the next place, another group that warranted special treatment were members of service units stationed outside of Canada but not overseas. Around the fringes of the continent there were units stationed in Labrador, Newfoundland, Kiska, and other places, which were from time to time engaged in combat duty. The position of this group was recognized by exempting them from half the tax that would have been payable had they been stationed in Canada.
These provisions covered the main elements in the tax provisions for the armed forces in world war II. They were the products of attempts to deal with specific situations as they arose, and represent one of the most unsatisfactory experiences in the history of Canadian income tax law.
My second heading refers to the inequities and anomalies created in relation to the rest of the taxpayers by the armed forces exemption. Even more serious than the problems involved in working out the tax positions of the armed services themselves
Income Tax Act
were the innumerable difficulties to which the exemption gave rise in relation to the rest of the taxpayers. The exemption for the forces was generally interpreted as being a reward for the risk they underwent in performing their duties and, as a result, almost every other group, both overseas and in Canada, that was engaged in an activity involving an element of risk sought similar preferred treatment. Outside of Canada the firefighters, the auxiliary services, the merchant marine, the ferry command, radio and press reporters at the front and other groups, at one time or another, requested income tax exemption in whole or in part. Some form of concession was finally extended to many of these, and I had something to do with working out those concessions, particularly with respect to the auxiliary services. At home taxpayers who were test pilots, civilian flying instructors, employees of shell filling plants, fishermen exposed to the risk of being sunk by enemy action, and even miners engaged in dangerous work underground producing metals for the war effort represented that on the basis of the armed forces precedent they should also be given some exemption from tax. As far as I can recall, no concessions were given to any of these groups in Canada but it was, and still is, utterly impossible to draw clear, logical and reasonable distinctions in this field. From the initial precedent of the armed forces exemption, claim after claim was made by groups who, in many respects, were performing duties involving equal danger, and who could be excluded only by holding to rigid and arbitrary lines of distinction.
The third, and of course least important, heading is the difficult administrative problems encountered in carrying into effect the armed forces tax provision in world war II. I think there I should point out that, although the principal difficulties encountered were problems of equity as between taxpayers, there were very serious administrative difficulties in carrying out this complex and cumbersome system. The mere fact that there were so many different graduations and classifications of taxability made the whole system most complicated for the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Revenue, and of course for the serviceman himself.
In the light of that experience, my belief is that any consideration which should properly be given to our servicemen who are serving in foreign fields should really relate to their remuneration and not to a tax exemption, if for no other reason in addition to the ones I have indicated here that such tax exemption is manifestly of far greater

Income Tax Act
value to the wealthy man or higher officer and of relatively little value to the man serving in the ranks. Perhaps I should add that the revenue implications are not of particular significance so far as the persons who are now engaged in Korea or who may later be serving in Europe are concerned. I was not in the house, but I believe the hon. member for Broadview made some suggestions about combat pay or something of the sort. It is not the function of the Minister of Finance to go into those matters, but if consideration is to be given to that type of service-let me say at once I do not say it should not be-
Is it going to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend could put that to the Minister of National Defence. I do not think it should take the form of an income tax exemption because such an exemption is of very little value to the ordinary serviceman and is of very considerable value to the high ranking officer or the officer who has a private income. It does lead to all these very difficult lines of distinction which I have outlined. I speak, as I say, with a very close personal knowledge of this matter because I had to live with it during the last three or four years during the war.

I appreciate fully the minister's earnestness in this statement he has made. Reverting to what he said towards the end of his remarks about an alternative, that is to say about combat pay, danger pay or whatever you want to call it-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It might, for example, be
called foreign service pay.

That seems to me a very practical point indeed, because I do believe that, as the member for Van-couver-Quadra has said, people's consciences are aroused. There is a great desire to have something done. Now, what is the practical thing to do? The Minister of National Defence is not here tonight, so is the Minister of Finance prepared to have this item left and, in the meantime, discuss this matter with the Minister of National Defence to see whether something can be worked out? While we desire to be co-operative I think there is no question but that the member for Van-couver-Quadra is right in saying that this is something to which the people wish to give expression. The minister has given a very formidable list of objections to income tax exemptions. Those of us who know something about the army, and about the way people get shifted or as the minister has said floated or flown into income tax exemptions, vividly describes the difficulties which arise.

Can the minister make a practical suggestion with regard to combat or danger pay, so that we will not feel this thing is being closed out? That is our difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will never be closed out. I shall be very glad to discuss that aspect with my colleague the Minister of National Defence. I have already indicated that I have no personal objection to that sort of thing. I believe that is the proper way to handle it, if something needs to be done. I recognize the feeling which has been referred to this evening. I do not think the proper way to give recognition to that sort of thing is by creating what I conceive to be a most inequitable and unfair way of giving a benefit to higher income people. If anything should be done, I believe the proper basis is something in the nature of, let us call it, combat pay or special pay for service'of this kind. I had hoped that we could have the benefit of discussion by some of our members who served in the last war under this system, because they will have seen the practical application of it.
I had hoped we might be able to conclude the resolutions this evening, but perhaps we cannot. I wanted to get the bills distributed. We can discuss this again on the bill. I do not believe we should hold up the resolution. For the reasons which I have given, and which I am convinced are sound ones, I do not think the income tax exemption is either fair or desirable. There probably are other ways of making provisions for what hon. members have in mind than the income tax exemption.
I am afraid that the minister is looking at this problem from the point of view of the last war rather than from that of conditions which exist at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Present conditions can quickly change to other ones, as my hon. friend knows.
If there is a change, then of course there can be a change here too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall the chain of events that I recounted in the last war.

The fact was that during the last war we had the utmost difficulty in persuading the Minister of Finance to grant any exemption at all. I remember our fighting over here, day after day; and it was extremely difficult to get him to grant any exemption. Finally, when the exemption was granted, it was only a half exemption; and to some of the groups to whom the Minister of Finance has referred tonight exemption was not given when, obviously, it should have

been given to them because they were risking their lives. What is the position today in 1951? We have a brigade fighting in Korea; and certainly anyone who is fighting in Korea should not be asked to pay income tax on the pay he is receiving for doing that fighting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The British brigade fighting in Korea are.
That may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the Americans.
Just a minute ago the minister was quoting the British the other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The British are taxed in Korea.

The minister talks about high
ranking officers. The highest-ranking officer we have in Korea is a brigadier.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be worth $172 a month to him.
That may be. The minister is being quite petty, I think, when he tries to base his defence on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should have said $142.91.
The government has a pretty weak defence when the best it can do is to try to throw a few bricks at the higher officers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no. I am just talking about fairness; it would be $6.85 for the privates.

There is a principle involved here, namely whether these men who are actually doing the fighting and are offering their lives in order to protect this country should be charged income tax on that pay.
I submit that Canadians from one end of the country to the other are against any such thing being done, and are perfectly prepared to make up the difference in taxation from their own pockets. The minister himself has said tonight that this question does not involve the revenues to any extent; there is not a great deal of taxation involved. But what is involved is the treatment of these young men; and that is a serious factor. This is a matter of principle, and not just a matter of a few dollars. I have here a letter written to the minister by a wife in Vancouver. I think it sets out the position clearly. It reads in part as follows:
Surely the men who answered the government's call to fight for our great nation, some never to return to their wives and families, should receive some small considerations.
In today's trying times of international strife, we must all come to expect higher taxes and restricted luxuries, to assist our country's great efforts toward preparedness. But why should our gallant men in uniform, fighting overseas, be expected to pay for the bullets they are firing, the clothes they are wearing, and the food they are eating?
Income Tax Act
That seems to be the picture from the point of view of the person in the street. I have here an editorial which appeared in the issue of April 28 of the Vancouver Sun, which is a supporter of this government. The heading is "Taxation where it Hurts", and it reads in part as follows:
Imagine the public uproar if the defence minister ordered our soldiers in Korea to buy their own bullets.
Yet that's just about the government's attitude when it insists that they go on paying income tax. This mean gouge is bravely defended by Finance Minister Abbott as the principle that "no group" should escape income tax.
Well, the men in Korea aren't just another "group" of Canadians. They're men who voluntarily gave up all comfort and safety in a time of high prosperity to risk their lives thousands of miles from home. Among the things they're defending is the freedom of other Canadians to stay home and enjoy the prosperity they've sacrificed.
There are editorials from many other papers to the same effect. I am afraid that the government is brushing this appeal aside because of administrative difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not.
The minister has stressed the fact that it is just too hard for the income tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister had stressed the fact that it is most unfair.
What about equality of sacrifice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
How much equality of sacrifice is there about that?

Most of the minister's complaint is based on the difficulties of administration:	they could not do this and they
could not do that, and therefore-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is not being fair. I put that consideration last, and I said it was far less important than the others.

All the way through the minister stressed the difficulties of administration. Not only did he do that, but there was also this argument about the higher officers, to the effect that they were going to get away with something and therefore they had to be taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A disproportion.

That type of argument is used only when there is a bad case to defend; and that is exactly what we are meeting here tonight. I suggest to the minister that further consideration be given to this question. I also appeal to the private members on the Government side of the house. They must

Income Tax Act
know, just as well as we do, that this thing is wrong. It is not a matter of partisan politics at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I completely agree.
Rot.
Who said "rot"?
I did.

You are the man who is talking rot. This thing is wrong. These men who are fighting for us should not be charged income tax on their pay. As to the men in the forces at home, different considerations may apply. I am not arguing now on their behalf at all. But I say that the men who have gone to Korea should be exempted from income tax on their pay, and that they should be so exempted at this session. That particular case can be dealt with. There is no excuse for trying to bring in other people in order to break down the argument made for the men in Korea. Let us deal with them and them alone in considering this question at this time. If that is done, I am sure that neither the minister nor any other member of the government can get up on the floor of this house and justify the levying of an income tax on these men who are fighting in Korea. It is eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move that the committee rise, Mr. Chairman, and report progress. I hope that, before we conclude the discussion of this section, we shall have the benefit of
the views of some hon. members who have had practical experience in this war. I would particularly welcome the views of the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Broadview; and I know there are a number of others.

In the last war, you mean.
Paragraph stands.
Progress reported.
